originalRequest: Produce the English variant of the shipped Chinese course learn-claude-code-skills for learn.agentmentor.dev. Teaching rewrite in English (not a translation): same 6-lesson structure, same lesson slugs, same interactive-block ids and answer positions, source quotes restored to their verbatim English originals from sources.md, natural desk-voice English prose with no AI-slop register.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The owner ratified the multilingual plan explicitly: all six locales on learn.agentmentor.dev, English first, batches of 2-3 courses in path order with a commit per course. The zh course is the verified source of truth for scope, learner model, structure, and grounding, so no additional clarification was needed.

learnerModel.targetReader: A developer who already uses Claude Code's basic features, understands basic Markdown and command-line operations, and wants to customize their workflows with Skills
knownConcepts: Basic terminal commands (cd, ls, mkdir, using a text editor)
Fundamentals of at least one programming language
The general idea of code review
unknownConcepts: How the description field triggers a skill
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: Claude Code installed, access to the .claude/skills directory, a text editor (VS Code or similar), and a terminal for basic commands
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: Identify one repetitive task in their own project that a Skill could automate
noviceRamp: Lesson 1 starts from a concrete pain point (re-explaining the same workflow) and uses a meeting-notes example to build intuition for why Skills exist
Lesson 2 dissects a real SKILL.md file part by part (frontmatter, instructions) instead of dumping every concept at once
Lesson 3 builds one complete but simple Skill (a task organizer) from scratch, with every step spelled out and copyable
Testing and debugging get their own lesson (4) so debugging complexity doesn't leak into the writing stage

learnerBrief: The target reader is a developer who already uses Claude Code and wants to customize workflows with Skills. They know basic Markdown and the command line and have programming experience, but they don't know what Skills are, how YAML frontmatter works, or how to write one. The course gets them to independently create their first practical Skill: understanding why Skills matter, mastering the SKILL.md structure, learning to test and debug, and studying real patterns through a code-review case study.
scope: Covered: the Skill concept and where it applies, SKILL.md structure (YAML frontmatter + Markdown instructions), writing the name and description fields, the automatic trigger mechanism, writing executable instructions, organizing supporting files, testing and debugging (direct invocation, iterative improvement), a code-review Skill case study, and personal vs project skills. Not covered: installing Claude Code, YAML syntax in depth, complex scripting, advanced language-specific knowledge, distributing Skills, or MCP integration details. Depth: from zero to independently shipping a production-ready Skill.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: No mermaid diagrams, matching the zh original. The core of learning Skills is understanding a text structure (YAML frontmatter + Markdown instructions) and writing concrete executable steps, so real SKILL.md code examples carry the teaching better than an abstract diagram would. Every lesson includes complete Skill file examples and step-by-step builds. The one candidate for a diagram — the test-fix-test loop in lesson 4 — reads clearly as an annotated list.
weakestPoints: Lesson 1's 'identify your first Skill candidate' exercise is open-ended; a beginner may be unsure whether their chosen task fits. Mitigated with explicit judgment criteria (repetitive, fixed steps, verifiable) and progressive hints
Lesson 5's code-review Skill spans multiple files and is the longest example in the course; it may feel heavy, but it exists to show real project completeness and is broken into modular steps
Advanced frontmatter fields (model, allowed-tools) are only touched briefly in lesson 6 by design (progressive disclosure), so readers who need them must consult the official docs

As an English teaching rewrite of a verified zh course, idiomatic drift is the residual risk: every source quote was restored verbatim from the English originals and checked byte-exact, but prose sections were re-taught rather than translated, so reviewers must check meaning-equivalence against the zh lesson rather than sentence alignment

acceptanceReview.terminalTask: The learner can independently write a complete SKILL.md (correct frontmatter plus concrete, executable instructions) for one repetitive task from their own work, invoke it successfully, test and iterate on it, and decide when a personal skill versus a project skill is the right home.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Four lessons carry one agentmentor-check block each (scenario fit in lesson 1, description quality in lesson 2, load-failure diagnosis in lesson 4, file organization in lesson 5), preserved from the zh variant with identical ids, modes, choice counts, and correct-answer positions; label, prompt, whyHere, choice text, and feedback are English teaching rewrites specific to each lesson's misconception. Exercises keep the zh Level structure with rubric, answer, and hints per Level, all pointing at the learner's real environment (their own project, their own code).
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: The course assumes no YAML knowledge (lesson 2 teaches the two required frontmatter fields from zero), no complex programming (examples are text processing and checklist auditing), and no language- or framework-specific expertise. Lesson 1's first exercise only asks the reader to reflect on their own work history and depends on nothing from unknownConcepts. Unknown concepts are introduced stepwise; the learner first builds a Skill in lesson 3, after all prerequisites have been taught.
